title: Municipal Christmas Lights Procurement: Writing an RFP or Tender That Works
metaDescription: Municipal Christmas lights procurement guide for Ontario: RFP spec language (IP44, 24V, aluminum frame), net-30, tax-exempt, warranty and delivery windows.
excerpt: A vague holiday lighting tender attracts vague bids. This guide shows parks and public works staff how to write measurable specs, evaluate bids on total cost, set delivery windows and decide between staff installation and a contractor.
heroAlt: Municipal park with large lit LED snowflakes, a giant star and pole-mount decorations installed for a town holiday festival
keyTakeaways: Specify measurable attributes (IP44 rating, 24V supply, aluminum frame, LED count, dimensions) instead of brand names or vague terms like heavy duty.
Ask for a line-item price sheet that includes spares, freight and optional accessories so bids compare on equal terms.
Write a delivery window with a hard date, and tie late delivery to a remedy such as a price adjustment.
Require a stated warranty period and a replacement-parts commitment for at least 5 seasons.
Decide early whether staff or a contractor installs, and procure installation separately if you use crews in-house.

body.text: Municipal holiday lighting purchases tend to fail in one of two ways: the specification is so loose that bids cannot be compared, or it is so brand-specific that it cannot be competed. Parks, recreation and public works staff who write a tight, measurable spec get cleaner bids, fewer change orders and a display that arrives on time. This guide covers how to structure the document, the spec language that matters, and the commercial terms procurement teams usually need, from net-30 payment to tax-exempt handling.

Your purchasing policy and thresholds govern the process. The suggestions below are practical guidance for the technical and commercial content of a bid document, not legal advice. Have your procurement office review the final text.
Start with scope: what are you actually buying?

Split the requirement into lots so suppliers can bid on what they do well. A typical municipal bid has four lots: pole-mount decor for downtown or boulevard poles, park or civic-square feature pieces, overhead street spans, and consumables and spares. Tell bidders which lots you will award separately and which you will award together.

items: Lot 1: Pole-mount decor, with quantity, size range and count per pole type. See [pole-mount decor](/product-category/pole-mount-decor).
Lot 2: Park and civic-square features such as 3D archways, giant ornaments and walk-through displays. See [3D displays](/product-category/3d).
Lot 3: Overhead spans and skyline decor, with span length and anchor details. See [overhead and skyline decor](/product-category/overhead-skyline-decor).
Lot 4: Spares and consumables including C9 bulbs, wire, plugs, clips and transformers. See accessories.

body.text: Spec language that gets comparable bids
Write requirements as pass/fail attributes that a bidder can verify on a data sheet. Brand names and subjective words invite disputes; numbers do not.
Electrical and weather ratings

items: Ingress protection: IP44 or better for all outdoor lit pieces, with the rating stated on the product data sheet.
Supply: 24V low-voltage operation with a Canadian-approved transformer (CSA or cUL listed), and the transformer wattage listed per piece.
Light source: LED only, with total LED count and colour temperature stated (for example, warm white 3000K).
Operating range: rated for Canadian winter conditions, with a stated minimum operating temperature.
Connectors: weatherproof, locking connectors on all outdoor power and data connections.

body.text: Structure and materials

items: Frame: aluminum, powder coated or equivalent corrosion-resistant finish, to handle road salt spray.
Mounting: includes brackets for the specified pole type, with bracket weight and wind-load rating supplied.
Size: stated nominal height and width, with a tolerance, such as plus or minus 5 percent.
Foliage and fabric: UV-treated and shatterproof, with flame-retardant documentation where required.
Weight: maximum weight per piece, so crews and pole owners can approve it.

body.text: A good rule is to ask for the data sheet to be attached to the bid and to require bidders to mark where each requirement is met. Mismatches show up immediately and can be scored objectively.
Commercial terms procurement will expect

items: Payment: net-30 invoicing from delivery or acceptance, with no online payment required to place the order.
Tax: bid prices exclusive of HST, with tax-exempt status handled by supplier on request, so your office can apply the correct treatment.
Pricing format: a line-item price sheet by lot, with unit price, quantity, extended price and freight shown separately.
Validity: bid price held for 60 to 90 days, so you can finish approval before ordering.
Volume pricing: unit price breaks at stated quantities, so you can scale up in later years without a new tender.
Delivery: FOB destination to a named address, with a stated receiving contact and a loading dock or lift gate noted.

See the [municipalities page](/municipalities) and municipal and parks overview for details.
Warranty, spares and replacement parts
A decoration that cannot be repaired in year three is an expensive disposable. Make the supplier commit to the things that determine lifespan.

items: Warranty: minimum duration in writing, with what is covered (LED failure, transformer failure, frame defects) and what is not.
Replacement parts: availability of transformers, controllers, bulbs and brackets for at least 5 seasons.
Spares: an optional spares package priced in the bid, typically 5 to 10 percent of LED sets and 10 percent of transformers.
Turnaround: stated lead time for warranty replacements during the season, ideally under 5 business days.
Documentation: wiring diagrams, installation instructions and maintenance guidance supplied with each lot.

body.text: Delivery windows and remedies

Delivery is the clause that most often hurts public displays. Pick a hard date and make it realistic: standard stock decor in mid-October, large custom or oversized items in late September to early October, with lighting night in mid-to-late November. State the window for shipments, the notice required before delivery, and who inspects on arrival.

items: Award by early September if you want installation to start in early November.
Require advance shipping notice 48 hours before delivery so staff can arrange a forklift or lift gate.
Inspect on receipt, photograph damage and note it on the delivery slip; set a 5 business day window to report concealed damage.
Define a remedy for late delivery, such as a price reduction or the right to cancel the affected lot.

body.text: Staff install or contractor?

Most municipalities already own lift equipment and have traffic control experience, which makes staff installation reasonable for pole-mount decor. Contractors make sense for overhead spans, large 3D installations and programs with tight timelines. If you split the work, procure the equipment and the installation separately, so product bidders are not forced to subcontract labour they do not control.

items: Staff install: lower cost per piece, but account for overtime, equipment time and seasonal staffing pressures.
Contractor install: ask for separate prices for install, mid-season service calls and takedown; require proof of liability coverage and safety training.
Hybrid: staff handle poles, contractor handles spans and large features.
Whichever you choose, ask the supplier for installation instructions and a pre-install checklist for each lot. A [professional installer](/professional-installer) can quote separately.

body.text: Site conditions and installation requirements
Many bid problems come from information the bidder did not have. Include a short site conditions section so suppliers can price accurately and propose pieces that will actually fit.

items: Pole details: pole material, diameter at the mounting height, mounting height range, existing banner arms and whether you want pieces mounted on one side or both.
Power: location of receptacles or feed points, circuit capacity, whether power is switched by photocell or by timer, and the required operating hours.
Environment: road salt exposure, snow storage areas, coastal or open-field wind exposure and expected temperature range.
Access: lift availability, working-at-heights requirements and any restrictions on lane closures or work hours.
Storage: where the pieces will be stored and what indoor space is available, so bidders can propose suitable packaging or reusable crates.

body.text: A simple bid scoring model
Publish the evaluation criteria in the bid document so bidders know what matters. A weighting that works for many public-realm lighting purchases looks like this.

items: Price including freight and spares: 40 percent.
Technical compliance with the specification (IP rating, voltage, materials, dimensions): 25 percent.
Warranty term and replacement-parts commitment: 15 percent.
Delivery schedule and reliability, including references: 15 percent.
Value-added items such as installation guidance, training and a spares package: 5 percent.

body.text: Adjust the weights to your policy. If you have an established vendor-of-record process, apply it first; if your threshold allows a quote rather than a tender, a clean line-item quote with the same spec language still gives you comparable numbers. Keep a record of how each bid was scored, since the same file will be your reference when you reorder next year.

One more item belongs in the bid package: a short training and handover requirement. Ask the successful bidder to supply a one-page installation guide per lot, a wiring and transformer pairing sheet, and a contact for technical questions during the install window. These cost the supplier almost nothing to provide, and they save crews hours in November when a piece does not light and no one remembers which transformer it belongs to.
Evaluating bids on total cost

Price is only part of the story. Build a scoring sheet that weighs unit cost with freight, warranty, parts availability, delivery reliability and compliance with the spec. A bid that is 8 percent cheaper but offers a 1-year warranty and no spare transformers can cost more by year three. Before awarding, ask for a sample or product photos of the exact items quoted, and check references from other municipal or BIA customers.

faq.q: What should a municipal holiday lighting RFP include?
faq.a: Define lots, measurable specs (IP44, 24V, aluminum frame, LED count and dimensions), a line-item price sheet, delivery dates with remedies, warranty and parts commitments, and payment terms. Attach product data sheets and require bidders to mark where each requirement is met.

faq.q: Can a supplier provide net-30 invoicing and tax-exempt handling?
faq.a: Yes. Municipalities and BIAs can request net-30 invoicing, tax-exempt handling and RFP- or tender-ready line-item quotes from Holiday Light Supplies. No payment is taken online.

faq.q: What IP rating should outdoor municipal decorations have?
faq.a: IP44 or better is a sensible minimum for outdoor low-voltage lit displays, which covers splashing water from any direction. Require the rating on the product data sheet and weatherproof connectors on all exterior connections.

faq.q: How long should warranty and parts availability be?
faq.a: Ask for a written warranty covering LEDs, transformers and frames, and a commitment to supply replacement parts for at least 5 seasons. Include a priced spares package so failures during the season can be fixed quickly.

faq.q: Should staff or a contractor install the displays?
faq.a: Staff are often cost-effective for pole-mount decor if you already own the lifts and traffic control. Use a contractor for overhead spans, large installations or tight timelines, and procure installation separately from product.
